fields.meaning: When, at the time  ~ | When, at the time
fields.connection: V plain form + とき / N + の / Na + な / Aい
examples: I put sugar in when I drink coffee.
When you are sick, you have to take medicine.
When I go to Japan, I take my passport with me.
When I went to Japan, I went sightseeing in Kyoto.
When I have free time, I watch movies.
When I was a child, I often played in the park.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes the point in time when something happens or an action is done.
Especially with verbs:
When using とき, we look at the order of the actions to put V 1 in the appropriate form.

V 1 た  : After V1, V2 （V 1 happens first）
V 1 る  : Before V1, V2 （V 1 happens later）
れ い１ ：
部屋を　出たとき、ドアを　閉めます。
When (after) I leave the room, I close the door.
The verb with とき is in the ta-form (出た), so 部屋を　出た is understood to happen first and ドアを　閉めます afterward.
れい２：
きのう、家へ帰るとき、パンを　買いました。
Yesterday, when (before) I went home, I bought bread.
The verb with とき is in the る form (帰る), so パンを　買いました is understood to happen first and 家へ帰る afterward.

～とき expresses “when, at the time” of a situation/point in time.
Key difference (verbs):
V-辞書形+ とき: the main action happens before/while V (before the completion of V).
V-た形+ とき: the main action happens after the completion of V.
V-辞書形+ とき: the main action happens before/while V (before the completion of V).
V-た形+ とき: the main action happens after the completion of V.
With adjectives/nouns: there is no “before/after” distinction; it only gives the time setting.
fields.notes:
With verbs of movement (行く、来る、帰る), choose 辞書形/た形 to distinguish “before going” and “after arriving”.
「このとき／そのとき／あのとき」 are phrases meaning “at this time/at that time/at that time (then)”.
「Nとき」 is not used directly; it must be Nのとき (例：朝のとき× →朝は/朝に or 朝起きたとき).
mistakes: Wrong point in time: ×日本へ行くとき、写真をたくさん撮りました（meaning after arriving）→ ✓日本へ行ったとき…。
Forgetting の with nouns: ×学生とき→ ✓学生のとき。
Using the wrong tense in the main clause makes the sentence hard to understand; be consistent (past/present).

rows: Indicates a point in time, neutral
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>にいました。
A relationship of inevitable condition, not a simple “when”
<ruby>春<rt>はる</rt></ruby>になると、<ruby>桜<rt>さくら</rt></ruby>が<ruby>咲<rt>さ</rt></ruby>く。
<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>のときに<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>してください。

examples: Tanaka: I'm going out tonight.
Tanaka said that they were going out tonight.
Tanaka said, "I'm going out tonight."
Miller: I have to go home early today.
Miller said that he had to go home early today.
Miller said, "I have to go home early today."
fields.explain:
Used to report some content.
Because it is usually used to report back what was said, it is often used in the past tense: 言いました。

examples: What are we doing about dinner?
What would you like to do with this box?
It's going to rain tomorrow. What shall we do about the picnic?
What would you like to do with the receipt?
How would you like to pay, cash or card?
Will you do this problem again later? — Yes, I will.
fields.explain:
Used to ask the listener to make a decision; the person asking is neutral.
In casual conversation: どうする？/ どうするの？
Polite: どうしますか; formal service language: どういたしますか。
Common answers are そうします/やめます/あとでにします/こちらにします.

Asks about a decision/the next action: “What will (you/we) do / how will (you/we) do it?”.
Usually follows a context/target that has already been mentioned (an object, a plan, a situation).
In service situations, used to confirm the customer's choice (payment, wrapping, delivery…).
Unlike どうですか (asking for an evaluation), どうしますか focuses on the action/decision.
fields.notes:
Sample answers in service situations: “袋は いりますか。— いりません。/ お願いします。/有料ですが どうしますか。— お願いします。”
In a group, どうする？ creates an atmosphere of discussing together; adding ね makes it softer: どうするね is dialect; in standard Japanese, どうするね is nonstandard; use どうする？/どうしようか。
In urgent situations: どうする？！ has a tense nuance: “What do we do now?!”
mistakes: Confusing it with どうですか: どうしますか asks about an action, どうですか asks for an evaluation/suggestion.
Missing context indicating the target: saying “どうしますか” on its own is hard to understand; state it clearly as “N は どうしますか”。
Use どうしましょうか when you want to make a suggestion; avoid どうしますか so as not to seem to force a decision.

rows: <ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>は どうしますか。
Focuses on “how is it/is it good”
この<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>は どうですか。
Expects the name of a specific action
<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みに なにを しますか。
<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>み<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>は どれに しますか。
Polite; the speaker takes part in the decision
<ruby>次<rt>つぎ</rt></ruby>は どうしましょうか。

examples: What do you think of these clothes?
How is life in Japan?
How about some coffee?
How about this seat?
How was your trip?
How is your homework coming along?
fields.explain:
Asks generally about quality/impression: どうですか has a neutral, gentle nuance.
Using は to mark the topic (N は どうですか) is more natural than を in this pattern.
In invitations: with rising intonation, in a context that calls for the listener's decision, it is understood as an “invitation/suggestion”.
Typical answers: いいです／だめです／大丈夫です／ちょっと… (a tactful refusal).

Asks for an opinion/evaluation of a person/thing/situation: “how is it?”.
Used as a gentle suggestion: “How about N?” → encourages choosing/trying.
The context determines the meaning: the same sentence can be an “evaluation” or an “invitation/suggestion”.
Made more polite with いかがですか (service, receiving guests).
Unlike どうしますか, どうですか does not require an immediate decision about an action.
fields.notes:
Use どうでしたか to ask about a past experience (past).
In service situations: “試飲はいかがですか” (Would you like to try a sample?); polite answers: “結構です/お願いします”。
Avoid repeating どう many times; replace it with いかが or specific adjectives (おいしいですか,便利ですか…).
mistakes: Confusing it with どうしますか when a specific action is needed; どうですか does not require a decision.
Using を with どうですか in invitations/suggestions: は is more natural (コーヒーは どうですか).
Using どうですか too directly in a formal setting; switch to いかがですか.

rows: この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>は どうですか。
<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>は どうしますか。
Polite form of どうですか
お<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>み<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>は いかがですか。
<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ませんか。
Softer than どうですか; often used when weighing options
この<ruby>案<rt>あん</rt></ruby>は どうでしょうか。

fields.name: ～は［language］で何と／どう言いますか
fields.connection: Nは + [language]で + どう/なんと言いますか
examples: How do you say 「猫」 in English?
How do you express this feeling in Japanese?
How do you say this sentence in Japanese?
What is Wi-Fi in Japanese?
fields.explain:
Formal: X は日本語で何と言いますか／どう言いますか。
Casual: X って日本語で何て言う？／どう言う？
The pattern “X は日本語で何ですか” is suitable when asking about a single word.
When answering, use: 「X」は日本語で「Y」と言います。/ Y と言います。

Asks how to express a word/sentence in a language: “how do you say it”, “what is it called”.
何と言いますか emphasizes “what is said”. どう言いますか emphasizes “how it is said” (the expression).
For single words/phrases, both 何と言いますか／何ですか are natural. For paraphrases/long sentences, どう言いますか is more natural.
fields.notes:
“何と言いますか” is often shortened in pronunciation to “なんと言いますか/何て言いますか”.
Do not confuse どう言う (how to say) with どういうN (what kind of N).
To emphasize the language: X は英語では何と言いますか（in contrast with other languages）.
Original notes: Spelling: 何と言いますか／なんと言いますか are both correct; なんて言いますか leans toward casual conversation.
Fillers such as “ええと/あの/その” often come before なんと言いますか to show hesitation.
When pointing at a specific object, the language can be omitted if the context is clear: これ、なんと言いますか。
To check a word you have just forgotten: 何て言うんでしたっけ (I forgot, what's it called again?)
mistakes: Wrong particle: ×日本語に何と言いますか → ✓日本語で何と言いますか。
Using どう言いますか for kanji: you need どう読みますか when asking how to read it.
Mixing up 何ですか (what is it) and 何と言いますか (what is it called); both are correct for single words but differ in nuance.

rows: X は <ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>で <ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>と<ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>いますか
「apple」は<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>で<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>と<ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>いますか。
X は <ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>で どう<ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>いますか
この<ruby>表現<rt>ひょうげん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>でどう<ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>いますか。
X は <ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>で <ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>ですか
これは<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>で<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>ですか。
Asks for the reading, not the meaning
この<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>はどう<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みますか。

examples: I practice every day, but I'm just not getting any better.
I can't get enough rest, so my cold just won't go away.
My homework just won't get finished.
I just can't catch a taxi.
My cold just won't go away.
My diet just isn't working out.
fields.explain:
◎ The situation is not progressing as the speaker expected.

Expresses regret at not being able to do something as one wishes, at not being able to succeed easily.

examples: I go home at 8 o'clock every day.
I'm going back to my home country this weekend.
I go back to my parents' home for New Year's.
When class is over, I go back to my room.
Today I'll get home late.
I go back to the dorm by bus.
fields.explain:
に帰る emphasizes that the destination is a place where one “belongs”; へ帰る is also possible but neutrally indicates direction and is less common.
帰る vs 戻る: 戻る means “go back (to the immediately previous position/state)”, not necessarily home.
帰ってくる/帰っていく: nuance of coming toward the speaker/going away from the speaker.
Often used politely in work conversations: 先に失礼して家に帰ります。

Movement back to the starting point/a place one belongs to (home, hometown, room, dorm…).
に marks a specific destination; 帰る expresses “returning” (unlike 行く/来る).
Has a nuance of familiarity when used with 家/実家/故郷.
Can be combined with a point in time or means: ９時に/電車で家に帰ります.
fields.notes:
“国に帰ります” is a familiar phrase for international students; often used with 休み/連休/旧正月.
Add a reason with ので/から/ために: 急用のために国に帰ります。
Different nuance from 戻る: 会社から家に戻る is usually unnatural; use 帰る.
mistakes: Using で instead of に: 家で帰ります (incorrect) → 家に帰ります.
Dropping に with 帰る: 家帰る (often colloquial, but in standard Japanese use 家に帰る).
Confusing 戻る and 帰る: 家に戻る (unnatural except in certain contexts); prefer 家に帰る.
へ帰ります is rarely the best answer on the JLPT; prefer に帰ります.

rows: <ruby>９時<rt>きゅうじ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>帰宅<rt>きたく</rt></ruby>する

examples: I'm going back home.
I'm going back to the office.
The holiday ended, and I went back to work again.
The weather has cleared up again.
I want to go back to my old life.
fields.explain:
“N + に戻ります” is used for both places and states (physical or abstract).
It is a neutral, polite expression, usable in everyday conversation and written language.
When talking about people, “戻る” has the nuance of “coming back on one's own”; when talking about things or situations, it can mean “returning to how it was”.

① Returning to the starting point: Expresses going back to the original place.
→ “return”, “go back”.
② Returning to a former state: Used when a thing, situation or mood goes back to how it was originally.
→ “return to the original state”, “go back to the previous situation”.
“戻ります” is the intransitive verb form of “戻す” (return, give back). The speaker goes back, or returns to some state, on their own.
fields.notes:
“戻る” can be used in both a physical sense (returning to a place) and an abstract sense (returning to a state, a frame of mind).
Clearly distinguish “戻る” (go back on one's own) and “戻す” (make something go back / return it to someone).
In conversation, “戻ります” is often used in the office: 例：「すぐ戻ります。」→ “I'll be right back.” (when stepping away briefly).
mistakes: Confusing 戻る（go back on one's own）and 戻す（give back, return something）.
Using the wrong particle: it should be に戻る, not へ戻る (although it is sometimes acceptable, “に” is more natural).
Confusing it with 帰る: “戻る” is used for a place you left temporarily and come back to; “帰る” is used for a place you belong to (home, hometown…).
JLPT N5–N4 often tests the difference between “戻る”, “帰る” and “戻す”.

rows: Return, go back (to a former place / state)
Going back or returning on one's own
Return home / to one's hometown / to where one belongs
Usually used for people returning to their “starting point”
Someone “returns” an object or a state
<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>棚<rt>たな</rt></ruby>に<ruby>戻<rt>もど</rt></ruby>す。（Put the book back on the shelf）
Emphasizes that the destination is “where one lives” or “one's hometown”

fields.connection: [place]に + Nが + あります/います
examples: There are students in the classroom.
There is water in the fridge.
Is there a dog in the park? — Yes, there is.
There is a computer on the desk.
This is a quiet town. The station is near here.
There is a meeting today.
fields.explain:
Typical word order: [Place] に [new subject] が あります／います.
が marks new information; は brings the topic to the front to emphasize the location: 図書館は駅の西にあります.
Politely asking where something is: 〜はどこにありますか。 For people: 〜はどこにいますか。
Very polite: 〜がございます（things/items in service, sales).

Expresses the existence/presence of a thing/person at a specific location.
あります: things, events, inanimate concepts (会議があります＝there is a meeting).
います: people, animals, living things. At the present point in time / temporarily in that position.
Possessive variant: “Nがあります” sometimes expresses “have N” (私には時間があります＝I have time), but for personal belongings 持っています is usually more natural.
fields.notes:
For robots/fictional characters that are “alive”: います is usually used (ロボットがいます) — depends on the context.
Detailed location elements: 上／下／中／隣／前／後ろ＋に indicate spatial relationships: 机の下に箱があります。
“Having time/an event”: 時間があります／試験があります — あります is still used because these are inanimate concepts.
mistakes: Confusing が/に: ✕公園が犬にいます → 〇公園に犬がいます.
Using を: ✕部屋を机があります → 〇部屋に机があります.
Confusing あります/います: ✕店に店員があります → 〇店に店員がいます.
Expressing possession: ✕私は車があります → 〇車があります／車を持っています.
Confusing です with あります: ✕机の上は本です（different meaning） → 〇机の上に本があります.
Order of counters: ✕三本の木があります（OK, but emphasizes N）; for existence it is more natural to say: 木が三本あります.

rows: <ruby>机<rt>つくえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>があります
N is the topic; emphasizes the location
<ruby>銀行<rt>ぎんこう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>の<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>にあります
<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby>を<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>っています
〜にいます vs 〜に<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>んでいます
にいます: temporary; <ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>んでいます: place of residence
<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>にいます／<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>んでいます
ここは<ruby>図書館<rt>としょかん</rt></ruby>です

fields.meaning: Expresses a feeling or evaluation （すき・きらい・下手・上手）toward an action; the verb expressing that action must be nominalized. Similar to 「～こと」.
examples: I like traveling.
I like running in the morning.
He is bad at driving.
I hate taking baths.

fields.meaning: Marks the subject of a modifying phrase
fields.connection: N1の/が + V/A + N2 (subject of the modifying clause)
examples: The café I like.
Is he the person I like?
Class A is the class with the fun teacher.
I brush my teeth before going to bed.
Please check the weather forecast before you go out.
I cleaned the classroom before class.
I'll be back before 3 o'clock.
Before going to Japan, I got a passport.
Let's wash our hands before the meal.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes preparation/a condition that must be done before another activity.
With habits/rules: ～前に～する has a nuance of advice/instruction.
Polite style: ～前に～してください／お願いいたします。
To say “don't do A before B”, you can use ～までVない or Vないで to show avoiding an action.

Expresses that action B happens before A takes place: A の/辞書形前に、B。
Focuses on preparation/conditions before carrying out the main action.
With a specific time, “X時前に” is more natural than “X時の前に”.
V辞書形+前に: A has not yet happened at the time of B (emphasizes that A is in the future relative to B).
fields.notes:
Vた +前に is incorrect; you must use V辞書形+前に because action A has not yet happened at the time of B.
With clock times: “X時前に” is natural; “X時の前に” is rarely used and sounds forced.
“以前（いぜん）” = “before, formerly” (the distant past); it is not used like “前に” to show an immediate sequence of actions.
mistakes: Wrong verb tense: ×食べた前に → ✓食べる前に.
Using “の” with clock times: ×3時の前に → ✓3時前に／3時までに.
Confusing it with うちに: “make use of the time while you are still free” → ひまなうちに, not “ひまの前に”.
Confusing it with までに: when emphasizing the deadline for handing in an assignment, use までに, not 前に.

rows: V<ruby>辞書<rt>じしょ</rt></ruby><ruby>形<rt>けい</rt></ruby><ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に
Emphasizes that A has not happened at the time of B
Emphasizes a deadline, not a sequence
<ruby>5時<rt>ごじ</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>
Emphasizes “making use of the time while still …”
Expresses the opposite sequence to “<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に”

examples: Japanese is hard.
Working overtime every day is tough.
Moving was a lot of work.
Getting up early in the morning is hard.
That must be hard. Shall I help you?
This job isn't hard.
fields.explain:
Use は to mark the topic being evaluated: N は たいへんです. To emphasize the subject in a sentence presenting new information, が can be used (with a different nuance), but the pattern here is は.
Use たいへんですね when hearing about someone else's difficulties, to show politeness and sympathy.
In casual speech: たいへんだ／たいへんだった.
Avoid using たいへん instead of むずかしい when talking purely about “how difficult the material is”. たいへん leans toward “hard work, effort, tiring”.

“たいへん” expresses a degree of difficulty, hardship or seriousness. Used to say that something is “hard/painful/troublesome”.
With “N は たいへんです”: a general evaluation of a subject, job or situation.
With “V の は たいへんです”: emphasizes that a specific action is hard to do.
In unusual situations/accidents, たいへん can mean “serious/terrible”.
The exclamation form “たいへんですね” shows sympathy/politeness in conversation.
fields.notes:
たいへん can be used as a polite adverb meaning “very”: たいへんおいしい、たいへん失礼しました.
Social formula: お仕事はたいへんですか (Is your work hard?).
To emphasize a serious incident: たいへんなことになった (Something serious has happened).
mistakes: Confusing it with むずかしい: “a difficult problem” should be 問題はむずかしい, not たいへん.
Dropping “の” when nominalizing a verb: ×勉強するはたいへんです → ○勉強するのはたいへんです.
Using が instead of は changes the focus of the sentence; with this pattern, keep N は たいへんです to state the topic.
Forgetting to use the polite/past form: たいへんでした (correct) instead of たいへんです (when talking about the past).

rows: <ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>はたいへんです。
この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>はむずかしい。
Spoken language, stronger than たいへん
たいへんに<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいです。

fields.meaning: Particle indicating the direction of movement. Often used with verbs of movement such as 「行く」「帰る」「来る」
examples: I'm going to Akihabara and Harajuku.
I want to go home.
I come here every day.
Where are you going?
